title: Mutual agreement procedure
summary: Article 25 lets a taxpayer ask the competent authorities to resolve taxation that does not follow the treaty. It also lets the authorities settle general questions of interpretation, consult directly, and, under paragraph 5, send unresolved issues to arbitration after two years. The 2025 update added references to the Transfer Pricing Guidelines' 2024 guidance for Article 9 cases, clarified when a case can be presented, and turned the GATS coordination rule into a new paragraph 6 of the Article.
readingNote: Saudi treaties generally follow the OECD wording for paragraphs 1 to 4, usually with a three-year time limit, and generally have no arbitration paragraph. Through the MLI, Saudi Arabia adopted the minimum standard allowing a case to be presented to either State (MLI Article 16) and corresponding adjustments (MLI Article 17). ZATCA publishes taxpayer guidance on how to request MAP.

entries.t: The Article sets up a procedure for resolving difficulties in applying the Convention in the broadest sense. Paragraphs 1 and 2 cover individual taxpayer cases, paragraph 3 general questions of interpretation and cases not provided for, paragraph 4 how the authorities communicate, and paragraph 5 arbitration of issues unresolved after two years.

Resolving cases of taxation not in accordance with the treaty is an integral part of a State's treaty obligations. Under the BEPS minimum standard (Action 14), States commit to resolving such disputes in a timely, effective and efficient way.
The Commentary clarifies and expands on the Article's general rules, drawing on the experience of member countries.

Competent authorities have broad delegated powers. Their mutual agreements, especially on interpretation, are relevant to interpreting the treaty under international law (Vienna Convention Article 31(3)). Some provisions expressly leave matters to them, such as dual-resident tie-breakers and recognised pension funds.
The procedure has two stages: the taxpayer's case with one competent authority, then the bilateral negotiation between both authorities.
It is a special procedure outside domestic law, available only for taxation not in accordance with the Convention. It does not replace domestic remedies.
Most cases involve double taxation contrary to the Convention, for example disputes over residence, the existence of a PE, or the classification of income.

MAP also covers economic double taxation from transfer pricing adjustments under Article 9(2) (corresponding adjustments). Even where a treaty has no Article 9(2), States should consider transfer pricing cases in MAP.

In Article 9 cases, including any arbitration, both States must have regard to paragraphs 6 and 72, and should consider paragraph 79, of the Annex to Chapter IV of the Transfer Pricing Guidelines adopted on 16 February 2024. Taxpayers should consider them in their submissions.
MAP is also available without double taxation, where taxation directly contravenes a treaty rule, for example a source State exceeding a rate cap.

A case can be presented before tax is assessed, once the State's actions make taxation contrary to the treaty probable, not merely possible. Examples: a change in law, a self-assessment return position the law requires, an active audit examination of the position where published positions or audit practice make an adjustment likely, transfer pricing reporting obligations where a corresponding adjustment is doubtful, and bona fide taxpayer-initiated adjustments. The test is applied from the taxpayer's perspective, and authorities should not demand domestic standards of proof.
Starting MAP early, on the mere probability of taxation contrary to the treaty, does not start the two-year period for arbitration. Paragraph 75 explains when that period begins.

A case must be presented to the competent authority of either State (the MLI minimum standard wording) within three years of the first notification of the action. Access to either authority helps ensure access to MAP.

States may instead require presentation to the taxpayer's residence State (or the State of nationality for non-discrimination cases), with a bilateral notification or consultation process if that authority rejects the case.
The three-year limit protects administrations against late objections. It is a minimum, and States may agree a longer period.

Time runs from the first notification of the action resulting in taxation contrary to the treaty, interpreted in the way most favourable to the taxpayer, normally the assessment or demand. Self-assessment and withholding cases are covered: for tax withheld at source, time runs from payment, or from when the taxpayer could reasonably have known of the issue.

The three years keep running during domestic proceedings, which can force a choice between remedies. Where domestic law allows, States may suspend the period. Alternatively, they may hold talks while domestic action is pending but settle only once it is withdrawn. The preferred approach is often to make MAP the first focus.

Without a special treaty provision, there is no general rule denying MAP for transactions seen as abusive. A tax charge under a domestic anti-avoidance rule is not a reason to deny access. States that want to exclude cases involving serious violations with significant penalties must say so clearly in the treaty.

Some States treat certain issues as outside MAP for constitutional or domestic reasons, which should be made clear in negotiations. There is little justification for relying on domestic law not to implement an agreement reached, since paragraph 2 requires implementation notwithstanding domestic time limits.
In the first stage, the authority receiving the case assesses whether the objection appears justified, a preliminary check of whether taxation contrary to the treaty may result.
If the problem stems from its own State's measure, it should grant relief unilaterally where it can. If it stems from the other State, it must start the bilateral stage.
MAP is available whether or not the taxpayer has also started domestic litigation. Whether a final court decision can be departed from depends on each State's law.
In the second stage the authorities negotiate. They must use their best endeavours, but they are not obliged to reach agreement.

The authorities apply their laws and the Convention. Where strict application blocks agreement, they may in a subsidiary way have regard to equity. Article 9 cases must have regard to the 2024 Transfer Pricing Guidelines guidance mentioned in paragraph 12.1.

Several bilateral treaties can together allow multilateral cases to be resolved, for example profit allocation among PEs in different States or integrated transactions in a group, and support multilateral advance pricing arrangements.
The last sentence of paragraph 2 requires agreements to be implemented despite domestic time limits. States that cannot accept this can set a time limit for the other State's adjustment instead.
Earlier OECD recommendations call for minimal formalities, published procedures, and the ability to present cases early.

If a court has decided the same issue for the same taxpayer, many authorities cannot depart from that decision, while suits by other taxpayers do not bar MAP. Taxpayers normally choose their route. Agreements may be conditional on withdrawing domestic appeals.
Audit settlements may limit access to MAP under some States' law. States should make this transparent, and settlements should not prevent MAP for the other State's part of a case.

Requiring payment of the disputed tax before MAP is not clearly barred by the Article, but suspending collection during MAP is desirable policy. If payment is required, refunds and interest should follow the outcome.

Interest and administrative penalties directly linked to a tax liability can be within MAP's scope. Penalties for separate compliance failures, and criminal penalties, generally are not. Interest and penalties should not be charged in a way that defeats the relief the agreement gives.

sections.heading: Paragraph 3: general questions and cases not provided for

entries.t: The authorities may resolve general difficulties of interpretation or application, for example by completing or clarifying an incomplete or ambiguous definition, settling questions of qualification, and agreeing practical procedures such as how withholding relief is applied.
Such general agreements are made by the competent authorities and bind the administrations until modified or rescinded.
The second sentence allows consultation on double taxation not covered by the Convention, such as triangular cases with PEs in third States.

Where domestic law does not allow the Convention to be complemented, the authorities may still agree interpretations within the treaty. They may also agree in advance to resolve multilateral cases under the first sentence.
The authorities may communicate directly, without diplomatic channels, by any convenient means, and may set up a joint commission whose composition and rules they decide.

Taxpayers whose cases go before a joint commission should have basic guarantees, such as the right to make representations and be represented, but disclosure of the case papers is not warranted. It may help to give the chair to an independent person.

If the authorities cannot agree within two years, unresolved issues go to arbitration at the written request of the person who presented the case, without needing the authorities' prior approval. Arbitration of Article 9 issues must follow paragraphs 6 and 72 of the Annex to Chapter IV of the 2024 Transfer Pricing Guidelines, including when proposing options and agreeing the sources of authority for the panel.
Arbitration is an extension of MAP, not an alternative remedy: it decides only the issues blocking agreement, and its decision is implemented through the mutual agreement.

The paragraph sets the essential conditions and leaves procedure to agreement between the authorities, using the sample agreement in the Annex. Some States put procedural rules in the treaty, as Part VI of the MLI does.
States may limit arbitration to certain issues, such as factual or transfer pricing questions, and EU States may coordinate it with EU instruments.

When a new treaty with arbitration replaces an earlier treaty that had arbitration, or that was covered by Part VI of the MLI, the States should clarify which arbitration rule applies to cases under the earlier treaty.
Arbitration should be available in all cases presented under paragraph 1. States without paragraph 5 can still agree ad hoc arbitration under paragraph 3.
The two years run from when the case was presented. States may lengthen this to three years, suspend the period while MAP is suspended, or restart it when material new information is requested.
Arbitration requires that taxation not in accordance with the treaty has actually resulted, not merely that it is probable. It applies only to paragraph 1 cases, though States may extend it.

States whose competent authorities can depart from court decisions may omit the second sentence of paragraph 5. Wording is given for suspending the two-year period while a court case or an agreed suspension is pending.
The period starts once all information required to address the case has been provided, and the sample agreement gives detailed start-date rules.

Relationship with domestic remedies: most States do not allow MAP and litigation at the same time, and taxpayers usually suspend or withdraw appeals to accept an arbitrated agreement. A taxpayer who does not accept the agreement may pursue domestic remedies, and the decision then does not bind the States.
Optional confidentiality wording for information exchanged during arbitration.

The decision binds both States unless a person directly affected does not accept the mutual agreement implementing it. Acceptance normally requires withdrawing litigation on the issues resolved. Optional wording puts this in the treaty.
A decision binds only on the issues submitted, but may guide similar cases. Some States let the authorities depart from it by agreeing a different solution within a short period.
The mode of application, including procedure, choice of arbitrators, costs and the type of process (final offer or independent opinion), is settled by mutual agreement. See the Annex sample.
Supplementary mechanisms such as mediation or referral to an expert for purely factual questions can be used whether or not arbitration is available.

sections.heading: Paragraph 6: relationship with the GATS (new Article text in 2025)

entries.t: Paragraph 6 deals with the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS). Under GATS Article XXII(3), a national-treatment dispute about a measure that 'falls within the scope' of a tax treaty cannot go to WTO dispute settlement, and a footnote limits this for treaties existing when the WTO Agreement entered into force.

Two issues: the footnote's limitation for pre-1995 treaties, and the ambiguity of 'falls within the scope'. An alternative provision included in the Commentary since 1995 now appears in the Model as paragraph 6.

Under subparagraph a), a measure falls within the scope of the Convention if Article 24 applies to it, and Article 24 covers taxes of every kind. National-treatment tax disputes therefore stay in MAP unless both States agree to take them to the WTO Council for Trade in Services.

States may prefer a narrower test limited to Article 2 covered taxes, or may have agreed to restrict or omit Article 24, with corresponding consequences. They may also define 'measure' in line with GATS Article XXVIII(a).

Disputes over whether a measure falls within the scope are resolved by the competent authorities under paragraph 3, or any other procedure both States agree, such as the Council for Trade in Services or arbitration.
States worried about timely resolution may provide a fallback procedure after an agreed period.
Similar issues arise with other trade or investment agreements. States may adapt paragraph 6 to keep tax issues in MAP, taking account of the tax provisions in those agreements.

membersNote: Paragraphs 95 to 95.4 are members' observations and paragraphs 96 to 103 are their reservations on the Article. The Annex contains a sample mutual agreement on arbitration. Non-OECD economies' positions are in section P(25).
